power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Rapid automatized naming (RAN) performance is highly predictive of reading outcomes when administered prior to the start of formal reading instruction.
Children with dyslexia struggle with this task and RAN difficulties are described as a main deficit in this population.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, some children with dyslexia also exhibit deficits in rapid auditory temporal processing of tones.
Given that automaticity tasks rely on speed, the goal of the current study was to evaluate rapid processing tasks, their relationship to RAN, and associated genetic variants of interest.
Children with or without dyslexia completed an assessment battery, provided a saliva sample for genotyping, and completed self-paced tasks of rapid auditory and visual perception online.
Children with dyslexia were significantly slower to respond during tasks that included a linguistic element (speech sounds or letters).
Performance on the visuospatial working memory task was correlated with rapid digit naming.

Among children with dyslexia, there was a significant main effect of a KIAA0319 variant previously associated with neural inconsistency on reaction times in the rapid speech task and a nominally significant effect on RAN performance.
Overall, we provide evidence for general processing speed deficits in dyslexia, though more research is needed to determine the relationship to candidate-dyslexia genes.

The ability to read is a fundamental skill that enables both academic success and daily functioning in modern society (Bretherton & Holmes, 2003; Boada & Pennington, 2006; Cassidy, Reggio, Shaywitz, Holahan, & Shaywitz, 2021; Raschle, Stering, Meissner, & Gaab, 2014).

text.text: Although most children learn to read with sufficient instruction and practice, approximately 10% of the population fails to acquire fluent reading and are diagnosed with developmental dyslexia (Snowling & Melby-Lervåg, 2016), though it is more prevalent within lower socio-economic status communities (Friend, DeFries, & Olson, 2008).

text.text: Individuals diagnosed with dyslexia demonstrate below-average reading ability despite normal non-verbal intelligence and adequate access to education (Peterson, Pennington, & Olson, 2014; Peterson & Pennington, 2012).

text.text: The development of the reading network requires rapid and automatic communication between the visual cortex and the language network to facilitate fluent recognition of letter-sound relationships and decoding of words.
Given the importance of fluency for reading, it is not surprising that assessments measuring automaticity of letter-sound relationships are highly predictive of future reading outcomes.

Rapid automatized naming (RAN) measures the ability of an individual to identify a grid of stimuli quickly and accurately (e.g., digits, letters) and is considered a primary deficit in children with dyslexia (Wolf et al., 1999).

text.text: Thus, the goal of the current study was to evaluate whether the RAN deficit correlates with more general processing speed deficits and if dyslexia-candidate genes influence these skills.
There are likely several causal factors, both environmental and genetic, that each contribute differently to behavioral deficit profiles in dyslexia.

For example, the variance in reading ability for those in high socioeconomic status households is primarily explained by genetic factors, whereas the same variance for those in low socioeconomic status households is equally accounted for by environmental and genetic factors (Friend, DeFries, & Olson, 2008).
text.formatted: For example, the variance in reading ability for those in high socioeconomic status households is primarily explained by genetic factors, whereas the same variance for those in low socioeconomic status households is equally accounted for by environmental and genetic factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Friend, DeFries, & Olson, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Given the complexity of the gene-environment interactions contributing to dyslexia, understanding the specific behavioral outcomes and mechanisms of these genetic factors is an integral step to understanding the complex nature of this disorder.

One approach to understanding genetic nature is genome wide association studies (GWAS), which have identified several candidate genes that are significantly associated with the disorder (Darki, Peyrard-Janvid, & Matsson, 2012; Galaburda, LoTurco, Ramus, Fitch, & Rosen, 2006 Mascheretti et al., 2017), the most studied among these being doublecortin domain-containing protein 2 (DCDC2; Chen, Zhao, Zhang, & Zuo, 2017; Marino et al., 2012), KIAA0319 (Mascheretti et al., 2014; Paracchini et al., 2008), roundabout guidance receptor 1 (ROBO1; Mascheretti et al., 2014), and dyslexia susceptibility 1 candidate 1 (DYX1C1; Rendall, Tarker, Contreras-Mora, LoTurco, & Fitch, 2017; Wang et al., 2006).

text.text: Each of these genes is suspected to contribute to the disorder's heterogeneity by impacting distinct and separate pathways that can each create the reading impairment that defines the disorder (Centanni et al., 2018; Galaburda, LoTurco, Ramus, Fitch, & Rosen, 2006; Hancock, Pugh, & Hoeft, 2017; Liebig, Friederici, & Neef, 2020; Mascheretti et al., 2017; Peterson, Pennington, & Olson, 2013; Wolf et al., 1999).

text.text: A more complete understanding of the genetic mechanisms underlying reading disability would provide valuable insight into the development of the disorder and help those seeking to optimize interventions for those with the disorder.

One such candidate gene that is associated with developmental dyslexia is DCDC2, a member of the DYX2 gene family that is located at the 6p.22 site of the human genome (Massinen et al., 2011; Meng et al., 2005).

text.text: The protein produced by DCDC2 stabilizes the microtubule structure of the primary cilia which allows for efficient and proper neuronal migration from the ventricular to pial surfaces (Galaburda, LoTurco, Ramus, Fitch, & Rosen, 2006; Wang et al., 2011).

text.text: Variation at this gene modifies or prevents the formation of this protein, which in turn leads to errors in the migration of these neurons, particularly the neurons located in regions that are involved in fluent reading (Burbridge, Wang, & Volz, 2008; Che, Truong, Fitch, & Turco, 2016; Marino et al., 2014).

text.text: Rodent models have been useful to understand some of the specific roles of this gene.

Work using these models has shown that DCDC2 variation is associated with deficits in processing rapidly presented stimuli, suggesting a potential RAN deficit when this gene varies in humans (Centanni et al., 2016; Truong et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011).

text.text: Four single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) of interest have been identified throughout the sequence of DCDC2, denoted as rs793842, rs1087266, rs807701, and rs807724 (Neef et al., 2017).

text.text: Those who have been diagnosed with dyslexia have been shown to vary at these specific sites in their genome more than their typically developing peers (Meng et al., 2005; Schumacher et al., 2006; Wilcke et al., 2009).

text.text: While the role of this gene is beginning to be understood at the cellular level, it is not known how variation in this gene, particularly at these specific SNPs, is related to behavioral outcomes.
Thus, it could be hypothesized that variation at any one of these SNPs may lead to a deficit profile that would not be seen in someone with variation at one of the other SNPs.

Another commonly studied gene, KIAA0319, has been associated with deficits in spelling (Neef et al., 2017), possibly by way of decreasing neural consistency to auditory stimuli, including speech sounds (Centanni et al., 2018; Hancock et al., 2017; Hornickel & Kraus, 2013; Neef et al., 2017).

text.text: It is unknown whether this gene's influence on neural consistency leads to poor RAN performance or if this gene is associated with poor rapid stimulus processing more broadly.

The goal of the present study was to investigate the potential roles of several SNPs in DCDC2 and one SNP in KIAA0319 in a sample of children with and without dyslexia on rapid stimulus processing and RAN skills.

We hypothesized that variation at the SNPs for DCDC2 would be associated with rapid processing skills as well as RDN and RLN behavioral outcomes such that those possessing a minor (risk) allele at these sites would perform poorer on these standardized measures compared to those with a major allele.
We also hypothesized that the KIAA0319 SNP would be related to rapid processing of speech sounds and tones, but not rapid processing of other stimuli.
Data were collected for this study during the COVID-19 pandemic, so all stages of this study were completed fully online.
We recruited potential participants through online postings (e.g., Children Helping Science, Facebook, Twitter, etc.) and screened for eligibility.
Screening for eligibility took place across two steps.
The study was approved by the Texas Christian University Institutional Review Board.

Parents provided informed consent by typing their full name into an online consent form prior to the collection of any data, and children offered verbal assent at the start of the Zoom session prior to completing any tasks.

First, parents completed a short background survey online on behalf of their child which asked questions regarding family and questions about language and reading delays, home reading environment, medications and diagnoses, and socioeconomic status.

Participants that (a) reported no history of neurological disorders, diagnoses, or medications, (b) were within the age range of 7 to 12 years old, and (c) native English speakers were then invited to meet with a trained researcher for a 45-minute Zoom session (Zoom Video Communications, San Jose, CA) to complete standard English neuropsychological assessments.

To be fully eligible for the study as a typically developing child, participants also (d) achieved a KBIT-2 Matrices (Kaufman & Kaufman, 2004) standard score of 85 or higher and (e) achieved a standard score of 90 or higher on each of four measures on timed (TOWRE-2; Torgesen, Wagner, & Rashotte, 2012) and untimed (WRMT-3; Woodcock, 2011) single word and pseudoword reading.

text.text: Children that achieved standard scores below 90 on two, three, or all four reading measures on the measures in (e) qualified as a child with dyslexia.
Children also completed the Digits and Letters subtests from Rapid Automatized Naming (RAN; (Wolf & Denckla, 2005)).

text.text: Of the 103 children that were evaluated for eligibility, nine were excluded for having a low KBIT-2 Matrices (standard score below 85), 22 were excluded for not having reading scores that fit into a typical reader or child with dyslexia category, and six were excluded for scheduling issues or not responding to follow-up emails.
Thus, the final sample included 33 typically developing children and 33 children with dyslexia.
All scoring was verified independently by a second trained researcher, and discrepancies were resolved by arriving at a consensus.
Participant characteristics are provided in Table 1.

text.text: After the Zoom session, children then completed four internet-based tasks at their own pace.
All online tasks were administered through PsyToolKit (Stoet, 2010 (Stoet, , 2017)).
text.formatted: All online tasks were administered through PsyToolKit <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Stoet, 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Stoet, , 2017))</ref>.

text.text: Children received a $20 electronic Amazon gift card as compensation.
The tone task was designed to exactly mimic prior work on tone discrimination as described in (Tallal, 1980).
text.formatted: The tone task was designed to exactly mimic prior work on tone discrimination as described in <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Tallal, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: In brief, children were told that two robots escaped the lab, and they were instructed to use the robots' beeps to identify them.
A 305 Hz tone was used to indicate a female robot and a 100 Hz tone was used to indicate a male robot.

Tones were presented in pairs (high-high, high-low, low-high, or low-low) and children reported the order of the robots' beeps (i.e., female-female, female-male, male-female, or male-male) using buttons on the keyboard.
Children completed eight practice trials with feedback and then practiced identifying the tones with feedback.
Children then completed 8 training trials on the sequencing task and 24 test trials without feedback.
Both accuracy and reaction time data were collected.

The speech task contained two stimulus conditions (consonant-vowel-consonant (CVC) and speech), each presented at four compression levels (full length, 50% compressed, 60% compressed, and 80% compressed).
The child was instructed to listen to an alien either practicing her speech sounds (CVC condition) or practicing sentences (speech condition).
During the CVC condition, children heard CVC syllables presented in a stream by a female, native-English speaker.
They were instructed to indicate whether the target sound 'dad' was part of the sequence.

During the speech condition, children listened to short sentences (e.g., 'Lemons are yellow', 'Dishes can whistle') spoken by the same female, native-English speaker, and were instructed to indicate whether the sentence made sense or did not make sense.
In each stimulus condition, presentation rate was blocked in sets of five stimuli each.
CVC stimuli were yoked to the speech stimuli by number of syllables and by correct response ('yes' or 'no').
Children completed 8 practice trials with feedback and 20 test trials without feedback in each condition.
Both accuracy and reaction time data were collected.
The rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) task included two levels of difficulty (one or two targets) and two types of stimuli (letters or shapes).
Conditions were blocked so that the easier level of difficulty (one target) immediately preceded the more difficult trials (two targets).
First, children completed five practice trials.
During single letter test block, children viewed 20 trials of 18 letters each at an inter-stimulus interval of 100 ms.
Half of the trials contained the target letter 'X' and half did not.
Trials containing the target were randomly interleaved with trials not containing the target.
During the two-target letter block, children viewed 40 trials of 18 letters that either contained no targets, the first target only ('X'), or both targets ('X' followed by 'O').

The shapes condition followed the same pattern as the letters condition, with the targets being a cross (target one) and a circle (target two) to mimic the visual characteristics of the target letters without the linguistic meaning.
Both accuracy and reaction time data were collected.
The visuospatial working memory (VSWM) task was designed to mimic an existing validated VSWM task used across the lifespan (Sander et al., 2011).
text.formatted: The visuospatial working memory (VSWM) task was designed to mimic an existing validated VSWM task used across the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Sander et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In brief, children completed a color change detection task in which they saw two sets of ladybugs and were asked to indicate whether the two sets were the same or different.
Difficulty varied across two dimensions: speed and working memory load.
For speed, the inter-stimulus interval between the two sets was either slow (1000 ms), medium (500 ms), or fast (100 ms).
For load, the number of bugs per set was either two, four, or six.
Stimuli were blocked by speed and load.
Both accuracy and reaction time data were collected.
Since this study was conducted remotely, eligible participants were mailed pre-labeled saliva collection kits.
The kits included instructions to not eat or drink anything for 30 minutes prior to completing the saliva collection portion of the study.
Of the 66 children that participated in the study, we received samples from 29 typically developing children and 29 children with dyslexia.

At the conclusion of the study, all samples were shipped to and processed by LGC (BioSearch Technologies, 2023) using allele-specific PCR-based KASP assay at LGC (Beverly, MA), with initial genotyping quality control and SNP genotype calls conducted using LGC's inhouse Kraken software and standardized protocols.

Genotyping was performed at four a priori SNPs identified in the literature as SNPs of interest for either phonological awareness (rs6935076 on KIAA0319; (Centanni et al., 2018; Neef et al., 2017)) or reading speed (rs807724, rs807701, rs1087266, and rs793842 on DCDC2, (Neef et al., 2017)).

In the current study, we report significantly slower reaction times during a series of rapid stimulus processing tasks in children with dyslexia compared to their typically reading peers and this effect was present regardless of whether the stimuli were linguistic (speech sounds or letters).
Interestingly, the reaction time differences were concentrated on the tasks that did include a linguistic component (speech sounds or letters).

Within the group of children with dyslexia, we observed significant effects of a minor allele in KIAA0319 (rs6935076) on RAN and on the rapid speech task reaction times, and only nominal relationships between rapid processing performance and variants on DCDC2.
These findings support the presence of general perceptual processing time deficits in dyslexia but will require further research to probe the genetic correlates of such deficits.
Rapid automatized naming is a speed measure, where performance is largely measured by the number of seconds required to finish the grid.
Although RAN measures are scored with respect to speed, performance on rapid naming may rely on cognitive factors other than perceptual processing speed.
A meta-analysis of 137 studies reported that RAN scores were most strongly associated with single word reading and text reading abilities (Araújo et al., 2015).

text.text: Given that reading is a complex skill requiring many distinct but related subskills, including phonological awareness, rapid automatized naming, working memory, and language (among others), it is not surprising that seemingly similar measures may yield different findings given differences in task design, and both rapid naming tests are used in clinical and research settings to study the same population.

Given these differences, it could be that poor RAN performance is due to a deficit in the rapid processing of perceptual information itself (Mascheretti et al., 2018; Visser et al., 2004) or due to other deficits such as poor phonological representations interfering with naming (Centanni et al., 2018; Hancock et al., 2017; Hornickel & Kraus, 2013) or an information flow problem between brain regions responsible for encoding the letter vs those responsible for linking the letter to its speech sound and name (Boets et al., 2013).

text.text: The choice of task, as well as the known heterogeneity in dyslexia, both behaviorally and biologically, likely impacts the nature and significance of the predictive relationship of RAN for reading outcomes.
First, deficits in visual or auditory processing have been inconsistently reported.

Prior studies reporting a broad rapid visual processing deficit have utilized visual motion tasks as well as attentional blink tasks (including those similar to our RSVP task) and prior studies reporting rapid auditory deficits typically utilize tone tasks.

Children with dyslexia exhibit deficits in rapid perception tasks, including those measuring tone order processing (Mascheretti et al., 2018; Tallal, 1980) and attentional blink (Mascheretti et al., 2018; McLean et al., 2011; Visser et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Children with dyslexia exhibit deficits in rapid perception tasks, including those measuring tone order processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Mascheretti et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Tallal, 1980)</ref> and attentional blink <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Mascheretti et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">McLean et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Visser et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Our tone and RSVP tasks were designed to mimic these prior studies.
In prior studies, when CTOPP RAN subtests were used, rapid color and object naming were significantly related to single word reading and fluency.

However, lower-level perceptual speed, defined as performance on tasks such as attentional blink (via an RSVP task) and go-no go reaction time, was associated with single word reading only (McLean et al., 2011).
text.formatted: However, lower-level perceptual speed, defined as performance on tasks such as attentional blink (via an RSVP task) and go-no go reaction time, was associated with single word reading only <ref type="bibr">(McLean et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the authors argued that low-level visual perceptual speed may contribute to reading independently of rapid naming ability.

Similarly, one study using multiple stimulus types reported specific deficits for stimuli that require accessing phonological codes (e.g., letters and digits) which contradicts the idea of a general rapid visual processing deficit (Ziegler et al., 2010).

text.text: Our use of the longer RAN/RAS form makes direct comparisons with these prior studies difficult and future work is needed to probe the subskills supporting each version of RAN.
A second possible brain basis for poor RAN performance could be increased neural inconsistency (i.e. neural noise; (Hancock, Pugh, & Hoeft, 2017)).
text.formatted: A second possible brain basis for poor RAN performance could be increased neural inconsistency (i.e. neural noise; <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hancock, Pugh, & Hoeft, 2017)</ref>).

text.text: Neural inconsistency is defined as decreased correlation between the neural responses across multiple presentations of the same stimulus (i.e., increased variance).

In the typically developing brain, it is important that the encoding of a stimulus occurs consistently over time so that the stimulus can be reliably identified in a range of conditions (e.g., high background noise, varying speaker accent, etc.).

Inconsistent neural responses to speech sounds make it difficult for the brain to associate an auditory speech sound representation with a visual letter (grapheme) and may therefore also interfere with RAN tasks that rely on knowledge of these relationships and automatic recall.

Up to 50% of children with dyslexia exhibit poor neural consistency and this neural feature is linked with variants on KIAA0319 (Centanni et al., 2018; Neef et al., 2017), which supports the current finding of a significant relationship between RAN and the same SNP on this gene.

text.text: Finally, poor RAN performance could be explained in a subset of the population by intact phonological representations but poor white matter integrity connecting visual and auditory regions.
White matter tract volume is reduced in children (Christodoulou et al., 2017) and adults (Boets et al., 2013) with dyslexia.

text.text: This anatomical deficit is associated with variants on DCDC2 (Darki, Peyrard-Janvid, Matsson, Kere, & Klingberg, 2014), and reduced white matter volume could restrict the speed of information in different brain regions to link the visual letter symbol with its associated speech sound.

text.text: In the current study, we did not collect neural imaging data, so we cannot speak to this possibility.
However, the lack of a relationship between DCDC2 variants and RAN indicate that more research is needed to investigate this possibility.

The significant nominal relationships reported here between both RAN subtests and a KIAA0319 SNP associated with neural inconsistency (Centanni et al., 2018; Neef et al., 2017) are an intriguing and unexpected finding.

text.text: One potential explanation for this finding is the importance of phonological representations in mapping letter symbols to speed sounds.
As noted above, the RDN and RLN subtests used in the current study were shorter versions that may load more on phonological awareness than higher cognitive ability (Norton & Wolf, 2012).
text.formatted: As noted above, the RDN and RLN subtests used in the current study were shorter versions that may load more on phonological awareness than higher cognitive ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Norton & Wolf, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, these measures may be more sensitive to picking up individuals with poorer phonological awareness, including those caused by increased neural inconsistency.

We observed significant associations between the KIAA0319 SNP and reaction times during the rapid speech/CVC task in the current study, which also supports the idea that some children in our sample may have had poor speech sound encoding, leading to an inability to process these stimuli quickly.
Future research should consider neural inconsistency and the role of KIAA0319 in tasks that combine phonological awareness with speed pressure, given this finding.
There is also evidence that this gene is related to RAN in other orthographies.

Interestingly, a large study in children learning to read in Chinese reported no relationship between genetic risk scores (13 SNPs in KIAA0319) and either phonological awareness or RAN independently, despite a significant relationship with reading fluency (Zhao et al., 2023) that was mediated by the child's RAN skills.

text.text: It was therefore surprising that none of the DCDC2 SNPs were significantly related to our current tasks that relied on speed, including a modified version of the task used in the rodent model study as well as standardized rapid naming.
There are a few reasons why these results appear contradictory.
The first possibility is that the tasks we chose to use in this study rely on separate, though perhaps overlapping, subskills that support passage reading.

Given that RAN scores are highly predictive of reading ability, we designed our tasks to probe whether RAN skills were influenced by more general rapid perceptual processing and unfortunately did not include a passage reading comprehension measure for replication.

Thus, the prior association between these DCDC2 SNPs and reading speed could be driven by other cognitive abilities not measured here and those that may not even load onto RAN, such as working memory.
Preclinical work investigating the impact of the rodent homolog of DCDC2 (Dcdc2) has utilized auditory processing tasks as well as learning and memory tasks.
Dcdc2 knockout mice exhibited not only significant impairments on rapid auditory processing but also deficits on working and reference memory during a radial arm maze task (Truong et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Dcdc2 knockout mice exhibited not only significant impairments on rapid auditory processing but also deficits on working and reference memory during a radial arm maze task <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Truong et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Our prior rapid speech sound discrimination task revealed significant impairments in Dcdc2 knockdown rats at rapid speeds (anonymized), which could be explained either by poor rapid sensory processing or by the working memory load added by processing multiple stimuli in rapid succession.

If DCDC2 interferes with working memory rather than lower-level rapid stimulus processing, it could explain why prior findings linked this gene with reading speed and why we did not see a relationship with lower-level perceptual tasks.
However, if DCDC2 is impacting working memory broadly, we would have expected to see a link between the VSWM task and SNPs on this gene in the current study.
Further, prior work in a transparent orthography did not find any association between two DCDC2 SNPs (including rs793842) and working memory (Riva et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Further, prior work in a transparent orthography did not find any association between two DCDC2 SNPs (including rs793842) and working memory <ref type="bibr">(Riva et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: It is therefore possible that the relationship between DCDC2 and working memory and/or reading speed is mediated by the interaction between this gene and others rather than variants on a single gene alone.
One strong possibility is the READ1 element (Powers et al., 2016).

text.text: Indeed, in the Riva et al. study (2019), which failed to link DCDC2 SNPs to working memory or reading skills, the READ1 element was significantly related to these scores (Riva et al., 2019).

text.text: Thus, future work on the genetic basis of dyslexia should prioritize the inclusion of mediating factors within and between genes of interest.

It is also important to note that prior work linking DCDC2 and reading speed included a large sample of children with diverse reading profiles, without specifically accounting for dyslexia in the population (Neef et al., 2017).

text.text: In our genetic analysis, we focused on the group of children with dyslexia, given this gene's association with the disorder itself.
To verify that results were not affected by excluding the typical readers, we also reran the analysis with the entire sample.
No SNPs were significantly related to our measures when the entire sample was included, the closest relationship being between rs793842 and RLN (F (2, 57) = 2.4, p = 0.10).
This study had four main limitations to address.
First, our sample was quite small in comparison to studies linking specific genes of interest to behavioral traits.
Although targeted studies in small samples can be beneficial for narrowing down genes of interest, results yielded from such small samples should be interpreted with caution.
Second, all computer tasks reported here were completed in the participant's home without a researcher present in any capacity.
This was done to decrease attrition during the already stressful COVID-19 pandemic, allowing children to take breaks as needed and hopefully maintain attention during the tasks themselves.
However, it is entirely possible that there were distractions in the home interfering with performance and/or other individuals in the home helping or otherwise participating in the tasks.
While tasks conducted outside the lab may be more indicative of real-world performance, they may be less comparable with prior in-lab studies.

Third, we did not include measures of passage reading in the current study, so although we did include timed single word reading, we were unable to assess how performance on our tasks load on to full passage level reading ability.
